defaults.permitted_development: A wraparound extension in England only stays within permitted development if the side and rear elements both satisfy Class A at the same time. In practice, many wraparound layouts need planning permission because the combined footprint, width or boundary effect stops the scheme being a simple side or rear addition. Councils usually focus on whether the work stays subordinate to the original building and avoids an overbearing effect on neighbours.

rules.height_rules: Single-storey wraparound elements should stay within the usual Class A height limits, with particular care on the side return where the 3m eaves rule can apply close to a boundary.
rules.depth_rules: The rear leg must meet the normal rear-extension depth rules, while the side leg still has to remain subordinate to the original house. One part of the design cannot compensate for the other.
rules.boundary_rules: Boundary relationships matter on both arms of a wraparound extension. The side return is often the tightest point, while the rear corner can create a stronger overbearing effect than a straight rear wall of the same depth. Councils usually focus on whether the work stays subordinate to the original building and avoids an overbearing effect on neighbours.
rules.roof_rules: Keep the roof simple and subordinate. A joined-up roof that creates a bulky mass around the rear corner is less likely to stay within the simpler householder route.
rules.materials_rules: Use materials that match or sit comfortably with the existing house so the combined side-and-rear form does not read as an oversized add-on. Councils usually focus on whether the work stays subordinate to the original building and avoids an overbearing effect on neighbours.

rules.permitted_development: In Broxbourne, the side return and rear addition both need to stay subordinate; if the wraparound form closes the side passage and consumes the rear garden in one move, it usually stops reading as modest householder growth.

rules.height_rules: In Broxbourne, height is usually controlled best by low eaves on the side return and by avoiding a continuous ridge that visually ties the side and rear together into one dominant roof.
rules.depth_rules: The rear leg still has to meet the normal rear-extension depth rules, and the side leg must remain proportionate to the original house. A wraparound layout cannot borrow tolerance from one element to excuse the other.
rules.boundary_rules: In Broxbourne, the boundary test is usually whether a usable side route survives and whether the combined side-and-rear form creates a long enclosing wall around the garden edge.
rules.roof_rules: Keep the roof simple and subordinate. Joined-up roofs that create a large boxy mass around the rear corner are more likely to need permission than a clearly secondary arrangement.
rules.materials_rules: External materials should match or sit comfortably with the existing house so the combined side-and-rear form does not look like an overgrown add-on. Councils usually focus on whether the work stays subordinate to the original building and avoids an overbearing effect on neighbours.

restrictions.conservation_area: Extensions in a conservation area often need a tighter design and siting assessment, especially on visible elevations or where the scheme would alter roof form, frontage or the rhythm of the street.
restrictions.listed_building: Do not rely on standard householder permitted development rights for a listed building. Listed building consent is usually required for works affecting character, and planning permission may also be needed.
restrictions.article4_notes: Article 4 directions can remove the usual householder fallback route in selected streets or heritage areas, so check the property's designation before relying on permitted development.
